title: M99, NGC 4254
caption: The spiral galaxy M99, imaged by the KPNO 0.9-meter telescope

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: We look straight down onto M99, a spiral galaxy of type Sc in the constellation Coma Berenices. Because it faces us, its spiral arms are on full display. The picture was processed, or "flattened", so that arm structure shows up both close to the nucleus and out toward the galaxy's faint edges.

Most images of M99 either let the bright center overflow into a white blob or stop before the dim outskirts appear. Compressing the range of brightness this way keeps both ends visible in a single frame.

M99 belongs to the Virgo Cluster of galaxies, the dominant cluster in our Local Supercluster, roughly 60 million light-years away. In 1848 Lord Rosse recognized its spiral shape, making it only the second such nebula known. His first had been M51, three years earlier in 1845.
scale: The Virgo Cluster, which includes M99, is about 60 million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: The 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak captured M99 in visible light, and the image's brightness scale was compressed to show both core and outer arms. The color mapping is not published.
understand.eye: A camera can record a far wider range of brightness than the eye picks out in a faint galaxy, and the processing here squeezes that range so the dim outer arms and bright center can be seen together.

explore: The 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory took this picture in February 1996. The Virgo Cluster also contains many other Messier galaxies, among them M49, M58, M59, M60, M61 and M84, as well as M85, M86, M87, M88 and M89, plus M90, M91, M98 and M100.
alt: A face-on spiral galaxy with clearly defined arms winding out from a bright center.
